figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Study design. $S$ is the fast surrogate; $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ are acceptance models. Paragraph edits pass invariant and blind semantic checks before surrogate-only search. All 5,321 inputs are fixed before target scoring; earlier original-paper scores are excluded from sampling and search. The human audit follows scoring. The miniature plots are schematic. ICLR denotes the International Conference on Learning Representations; AUC, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; CPU, central processing unit. LLM denotes large language model; bfloat16 is a reduced-precision numerical format. In the schematic, $\Delta$ denotes a score change, $\rho$ Spearman’s rank correlation (Spearman, 1904), $G$ the adaptive-minus-random target gain, and $Q$ the maximum number of surrogate evaluations; Opus and Sol denote Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1-Sol.
figures.headline: Three studies share one fixed set of 5,321 scored inputs, with all edits checked before any target scores them.
citing_sentences: We fix every evaluation text and its order before target scoring (Figure 1).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Surrogate changes barely track target changes for the same edits. (a, b) Density of all 3,323 admitted single edits across 199 papers: surrogate change against the change for $T_{1}$ (a) and $T_{2}$ (b) in the post hoc 32-bit rescoring of the released weights, each in units of its evaluator’s standard deviation (SD) across unedited papers (the 328 frozen originals for $S$; the 200 Study 2 originals, in 32-bit, for the targets); darker bins hold more edits (log scale). The axes use different standardized ranges because the surrogate moves far less. The inset gives the mean within-paper Spearman correlation (Spearman, 1904) with its 95% paper-bootstrap confidence interval (CI); Table 4 gives these 32-bit estimates and the pre-specified bfloat16 ones. (c) Within-paper correlations for the 198 eligible papers between $S$ and each target and, right of the dotted rule, between the two targets (post hoc, 32-bit; points, offset horizontally so equal values stay visible), with their mean and 95% CI (outlined marker).
figures.headline: Surrogate score changes barely track the targets' changes on the same edits, and target-to-target correlations are weak.
citing_sentences: On the same 198 papers, their original-paper correlation is 0.603, while their post hoc 32-bit edit agreement is $0.047\;[0.004,\,0.090]$ (Table 4; Figure 2c).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Proxy choices give little average advantage in equal-size five-edit banks (post hoc). (a, b) Chosen target change minus the exact uniform-random mean of the same sampled bank, for surrogate choice, sibling choice, and the evaluated target’s oracle choice. Open markers denote proxy choices; filled markers denote the outcome-informed oracle. Estimates average 1,000 draws within each of 198 papers; intervals are nominal 95% paper-bootstrap confidence intervals. Target changes are the 32-bit rescoring of the released weights, in units of each target’s 32-bit standard deviation (SD) across the 200 Study 2 originals; bfloat16 values are in Supplementary Table S11. (c, d) Empirical cumulative distributions of paperwise oracle-minus-choice regret, averaged over those same draws; solid lines use the surrogate, dashed lines the sibling. The intervals are conditional on the existing edit banks and exclude Monte Carlo subsampling error, which Supplementary Section S6 quantifies.
figures.headline: Choosing with a surrogate or sibling gives no measurable average advantage over random choice, while oracle choice does.
citing_sentences: Neither $S$ nor the sibling model shows a measurable average advantage over random choice (Figure 3a, b).
The score lost by choosing with a proxy rather than the evaluated target also varies by paper (Figure 3c, d); in 32-bit, its mean for surrogate choice is 0.078 SD on $T_{1}$ and 0.054 SD on $T_{2}$.

figures.label: Figure S1
figures.caption: Prediction and inference-cost context. AUC denotes area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; CI denotes confidence interval; CPU and GPU denote central and graphics processing units. (a) AUC on the common 1,667-paper original-text benchmark, with nominal 95% CIs. (b) Median inference time from extracted text, on a CPU for $S$ and one RTX 4090 GPU for $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$. The CPU median uses the first 200 benchmark papers; target medians use all 5,321 frozen inputs. Different processors and timing cohorts make this a practical cost comparison, not an isolated architectural speedup measurement.
figures.headline: Surrogate inference is far faster than target inference, while the three evaluators' AUC values are close to one another.

figures.label: Figure S2
figures.caption: Automated admission and blind human validity are different measurements. (a) Share of proposed items admitted by the automated checks, with the number of checkable proposals at the right; composite endpoints receive a further whole-document semantic check. (b) Share of admitted items judged valid in the later blind human audit, with the counts at the right and exact two-sided 95% binomial confidence intervals (CIs); an unsure judgment counts as not valid. The audit samples 59 endpoints, 20 presentation edits, and 20 evidence removals. These are conditional samples of admitted items and cannot be compared directly with generation pass rates as if they shared a denominator. $Q$ is the maximum number of surrogate evaluations allowed to the search.
figures.headline: Automated admission and blind human validity measure different things, with the human audit judging all sampled endpoints valid.
citing_sentences: Passing the automated checks is only the first test of preservation (Supplementary Figure S2a).

figures.label: Figure S3
figures.caption: The removal-minus-sham estimates are imprecise and confounded by coherence defects. One panel per evaluator. The first two rows show separate mean changes from the original for admitted evidence removals (102 papers) and length-matched shams (184 papers). The row below the dotted rule is the within-paper removal-minus-sham contrast on the 93 paired papers; it is not the difference between the first two means, which use different cohorts. Effects use each evaluator’s original-score standard deviation (SD), with nominal 95% paper-bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) and point estimates above the marks. Human auditing finds coherence defects in six of 20 sampled removals, limiting a pure evidence-ablation interpretation.
figures.headline: Evidence removals and matched shams show no clearly separated score changes, and six of 20 audited removals had coherence defects.
citing_sentences: On these paired papers, the removal-minus-sham contrast is $0.000\;[-0.012,\,0.012]$ SD for $S$, $-0.031\;[-0.073,\,0.011]$ for $T_{1}$, and $-0.028\;[-0.059,\,0.002]$ for $T_{2}$ (Figure S3).

figures.label: Figure S4
figures.caption: Restricting edits to fully visible paragraphs leaves mean edit agreement near zero (post hoc). (a, b) Mean within-paper Spearman correlation (Spearman, 1904) for $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$, using all eligible edits (open markers) or only paragraphs wholly retained by both targets and the surrogate’s lexical window (filled markers). Both rows contain the same 198 papers: 3,321 edits before filtering and 3,072 after. Intervals are nominal 95% paper-bootstrap confidence intervals; original estimates retain their original intervals. (c, d) Each paper’s correlation before and after filtering, with the identity line in gray. Overlapping points remain superimposed. The filter retains visible changed spans while leaving different surrounding model contexts and whole-document surrogate features intact; it is not an equalized-context experiment.
figures.headline: Restricting edits to fully visible paragraphs leaves mean edit agreement near zero for both targets.
citing_sentences: Restricting the analysis to paragraphs visible to all scorers leaves agreement near zero (Supplementary Table S8 and Figure S4).

figures.label: Figure S5
figures.caption: Adaptive search has a small average source advantage, variable target effects, and unequal realized consumption. (a) Adaptive minus best-of-$Q$ random gain at each maximum allowance, with both policies selecting according to $S$; the original remains eligible. Only the two target contrasts at $Q=512$ belong to the four-test family. Shading marks exploratory budgets; budgets $Q=1$ and $Q=8$ lack complete endpoint checks. (b) Empirical cumulative distributions of the 128 paperwise contrasts at 512, with win/tie/loss counts below. Columns show $S$, $T_{1}$, and $T_{2}$ in their own original-score standard deviation (SD) units on shared axes. (c) Actual candidate evaluations recovered by exact replay, with seeds averaged within each paper; points are vertically offset for visibility and diamonds mark medians. Intervals in (a) are the original nominal 95% paper-bootstrap confidence intervals; (b, c) are post hoc descriptions of observed variation. Invalid checked endpoints contribute zero gain.
figures.headline: Adaptive search gives a small average advantage over random search, with variable target effects and unequal evaluation use.
citing_sentences: At the pre-specified maximum budget of 512, adaptive search does not measurably outperform random search on either target, in bfloat16 or in 32-bit (Table 4); other budgets are exploratory (Supplementary Figure S5).
At 512, we average the two seeds within each paper and plot the distribution of adaptive-minus-random changes (Figure S5b).

figures.label: Figure S6
figures.caption: Original-relative controls retain the small source-objective advantage and the uncertainty of target changes. Changes from the original for adaptive search, random search, and filtered one-pass polish. Columns show $S$, $T_{1}$, and $T_{2}$, each standardized by its own original-score standard deviation (SD). Intervals are the original nominal 95% paper-bootstrap confidence intervals, averaging the two search seeds within each of 128 papers. Invalid checked endpoints count as zero gain. The polishing contrasts are descriptive.
figures.headline: Original-relative changes keep the small surrogate advantage, while target gains from either search policy have intervals that include zero.
citing_sentences: Figure S6 supplies the original-relative controls, including polishing.

figures.label: Figure S7
figures.caption: Larger banks increase oracle advantage without a clear proxy advantage on the fixed cohort (post hoc). Panels show $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ on the same 160 papers with at least fifteen admitted edits. Lines compare surrogate, sibling, and outcome-informed oracle choice against the uniform-random expectation of the same sampled bank, at five, ten, and fifteen edits. Each estimate averages 1,000 draws within paper before a 10,000-resample paper bootstrap; intervals are nominal 95% confidence intervals. Units are target original-score standard deviations (SDs). The oracle’s positive advantage reflects selection by construction. Fixed cohort membership prevents changing paper composition from explaining its increase.
figures.headline: Larger banks raise the oracle's advantage on a fixed cohort, while surrogate and sibling intervals still span zero at five, ten, and fifteen edits.
citing_sentences: Larger candidate sets increase the oracle’s advantage, but not the proxies’ measurable advantage, on a fixed cohort (Supplementary Figure S7).
Figure S7 holds that cohort constant.

Increasing the sampled bank size from five to fifteen on the same 160 papers increases the oracle advantage, while all surrogate- and sibling-choice intervals still span zero (Supplementary Figure S7).

abstract: A fast acceptance classifier could select revisions for a slower evaluator. We ask whether agreement on existing papers supports that use. We compare a classifier of word and document features with two released text-only acceptance predictors fine-tuned from the same language model with three billion parameters. For 198 papers from the International Conference on Learning Representations, we compare model rankings of the original papers and of paragraph rewrites screened automatically for unchanged facts, claim strength, and attribution. The classifier ranks original papers closely with one predictor and moderately with the other, but shows no detectable agreement with either on which rewrites raise scores. The tests specified in advance used reduced numerical precision. Rounding error dominated the small score responses. We therefore rescored the released weights in full 32-bit precision as a post hoc check; edit agreement remained near zero. At this precision, when each predictor chooses among five rewrites per paper, its average raw score is under two points out of 100 higher than with random choice. The evidence covers presentation rewrites and two open predictors from one family; transfer to costly evaluators remains untested. Revision selectors should therefore be checked against the intended evaluator on the revisions they rank.

sections.body: The paper asks whether a cheap text classifier, called the surrogate S, can select revisions for two acceptance predictors, T1 and T2, which share a three billion parameter base model. Edits are chosen by S alone, and neither target guides generation or selection. Original-paper agreement may not carry over to revisions, since two reviewers can agree on original scores yet disagree on whole-paper revision gains. Single-paragraph rewrites allow several alternatives to be compared within each paper. Figure 1 maps three studies, and all scored inputs are fixed before target scoring. The authors state that the selection setting is hypothetical and that transfer to costly evaluators remains untested.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Predicting acceptance does not show which paragraph rewrites an evaluator rewards, so this paper tests that agreement directly.

sections.body: The surrogate S is logistic regression on TF-IDF word features and document counts, trained on 21,141 PaperScorer training papers. The targets are PaperScorer-3B-Text-OpenReview-ICLR (T1) and PaperScorer-3B-Text-arXiv (T2), both fixed fine-tunes of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. Edits are paragraph rewrites by GPT-6-Luna, admitted only if they pass an invariant check and a semantic check by GPT-6.1-Sol. The pre-specified target scores use bfloat16, and the authors also rescore the released weights in 32-bit as a post hoc check. Edit fidelity is the mean within-paper Spearman correlation between surrogate and target score changes.
sections.heading: Evaluators and study design
sections.headline: A logistic regression surrogate and two released predictors score frozen paragraph-rewrite inputs under four pre-specified tests.

sections.body: The writer was instructed to keep numbers, citations, and claim strength fixed, and the automated checks are an invariant check plus a semantic check. The two checks admit 70.5% of checkable Study 2 paragraph edits but only 102 of 198 evidence removals. A second provider agrees with the primary checker on 86.6% of 1,323 rechecked items. In a blind audit by one author, all 59 endpoints and all 20 presentation edits were judged valid, with exact one-sided 95% upper bounds on invalidity of 4.95% and 13.9%. Six of 20 evidence removals were judged invalid, mostly from coherence problems. The audit has one rater, and no check estimates the miss rate for natural edits.
sections.heading: How often are the proposed edits valid?
sections.headline: Automated checks admit 70.5% of checkable paragraph edits, and a blind audit judges all sampled presentation edits valid.

sections.body: The pre-specified bfloat16 analysis covers 198 papers with at least five admitted edits. Mean within-paper correlations are -0.008 for T1 and -0.015 for T2, with nominal upper limits of 0.025 and 0.022. The null persists for a dense surrogate that reads word order, while a regularized predictor recovers the surrogate's own changes poorly. In 32-bit, the edit-fidelity estimates remain near zero. Mean absolute responses range from 1.0 to 1.4 raw-score points out of 100. Adaptive search at 512 evaluations does not measurably outperform random search on either target. Cross-GPU rescoring reproduces 32-bit edit changes almost exactly, with correlations of 0.9997 and 0.9998 on 25 papers.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Surrogate edit rankings show no detectable agreement with either target, and search gains stay near zero.

sections.body: This section places the study among acceptance predictors, peer-review resources, and adversarial transfer work. PeerRead paired submissions with decisions (Kang et al., 2018), and IteraTeR and arXivEdits annotate edit intentions. Table 5 compares the closest studies. Yang et al. (2026b) reports across-paper Pearson correlations of 0.804 on original scores and 0.085–0.415 on revision gains. The authors note that PaperScorer's own section-edit gains of 3.9–6.1% differ in unit from raw-score points. Prior transfer results involve presentation-only revisions and adversarial abstract rewrites optimized against reviewers that read the same text. The authors argue that their contribution is the measurement rather than the phenomenon.
sections.heading: Related work
sections.headline: Related work on review feedback and text manipulation does not measure within-paper agreement between scorers on paragraph edits.

sections.body: The authors argue that paper prediction and edit response can depend on different textual properties, since the checks hold most document-structure counts fixed. Acceptance labels are noisy and record paper-level decisions, not preferences among presentation rewrites. Input length is a further limit: restricting edits to paragraphs visible to all scorers leaves agreement near zero. The evidence covers one sparse surrogate, one writer configuration, English ICLR papers, and two predictors from one base model. A DeepReviewer-14B check, run in an 8-bit version not validated against the original weights, also shows no edit-ranking agreement. The authors state that revision tools should be tested on the changes they are meant to guide.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Agreement on original papers does not carry over to revisions, and the findings cover only presentation-only paragraph rewrites.

sections.body: The surrogate ranks original papers closely with one target and moderately with the other, yet shows no detectable agreement with either on which rewrites raise scores. The two targets barely agree on edits. Choosing edits with the surrogate gives no detectable advantage over random choice. Choosing the best of five with a predictor's own score raises it by under two points in 32-bit, more than twice the mean change from an added space. The authors state that these results bound agreement for checker-admitted rewrites rather than show that either predictor is wrong. Agreement between models does not establish valid edit preferences.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The surrogate tracks original-paper rankings but not checked rewrites, so revision tools should be validated against their intended evaluators.

sections.body: The broader impact statement notes that automated paper scores can shape author effort and research assessment. A cheap classifier's agreement with acceptance predictors on existing papers did not indicate which revisions those predictors reward. A constrained search raised the classifier's own score by about 0.06 SD without detectably raising the predictors' scores. The authors suggest testing feedback tools on controlled revisions rather than relying on their scores alone for publication decisions. Apart from this article and two licensed example paragraphs, the planned release contains no manuscript text.
sections.heading: Broader impact statement
sections.headline: The paper warns that automated scores should not alone guide publication decisions, and its planned release contains no author-facing optimizer.

sections.body: Analysis code, paper identifiers, edit types and positions, scores, and experiment logs are to be released in a public GitHub repository named Ranking-Agreements once the arXiv preprint is available. Original and edited manuscript text will not be redistributed publicly, except the two licensed examples in Supplementary Section S2.6. The frozen inputs are available to the editor and reviewers on request for verification only. The released per-edit scores reproduce Table 4 without the texts. PaperScorer's dataset and model cards state custom or other licensing, so the authors do not treat them as freely redistributable. DeepReviewer use is subject to its model license.
sections.heading: Data and code availability
sections.headline: Analysis code and per-edit scores will be public, while manuscript text stays restricted to the editor and reviewers.

sections.body: The appendix gives the surrogate's feature set and its validation AUC of 0.691, along with the exclusion rules that leave 860 editing candidates. It lists target prompts and the decision readout, the search algorithms with budget accounting, and the writer and checker rules. Table S17 gives model revisions and software versions. The cost accounting records approximately 37.68 million input tokens and 28.77 hours of summed duration for successful OpenAI-based attempts. It also lists departures from the initial design, including dropped whole-paper rewrite conditions and an omitted human anchor.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists configurations, prompts, search algorithms, model versions, sampling rules, and cost accounting for the study.
